newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican troops closely watch wake for druglord.
newsitem.headline: Mexican troops closely watch wake for druglord.

text.p: Dozens of Mexican troops and anti-drugs agents searched mourners for weapons on Friday as they left an all-night wake for Mexico's most wanted druglord, Amado Carrillo Fuentes.
A truckload of heavily armed troops backed by an armoured personnel carrier set up a roadblock to stop guests as they left the vigil being held at the luxury ranch of Carrillo's family.
"They are seeing if we have got any weapons, but of course we don't,' an enraged woman, who declined to give her name, told Reuters.
It was the latest setback for the family of Carrillo, whose body was seized last Saturday by Mexican authorities as soon as the druglord's mother had identified him.
He died the day before under mysterious circumstances following extensive plastic surgery that authorities said was a desperate attempt to change his appearance to avert capture.

Although U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration officials identified the body almost immediately, Mexican authorities waited until they received the results of DNA tests on Thursday to ensure Carrillo had not faked his own death.
U.S. officials considered Carrillo the most important figure in the Mexican drug trade, shipping tonnes of cocaine a year to the United States from his base in northern Mexico.

Carrillo, the so-called "Lord of the Skies", was head of the Juarez drug cartel and earned his nickname from the huge air shipments of Colombian cocaine he flew to Mexico and shipped across the United States border.

At the meticulously-kept ranch where his mother held the wake on Friday, family friends allowed dozens of reporters to enter the compound at 2 a.m./4 a.m. EDT (0800 GMT) in a bid to prevent soldiers from storming the heavily-guarded residence.
"If it hadn't been for all the journalists, the army would have entered," Carlos Soto, a childhood friend of Carrillo, told Reuters.

Fearing searches, about 70 local people and family friends remained inside the ranch overnight where the druglord's decomposed body was on display in an open coffin -- although out of view from the media.
His relatives were heard wailing in grief inside the ranch house and dozens of wreaths -- some of them reportedly sent by rival drug kingpins -- lay against the outside wall.
Carrillo was due to be buried on Friday in a private ceremony.

The last big Carrillo family gathering was the wedding of his younger sister Aurora in January. The druglord attended the festivities, which were stormed by military and crack police units searching for Carrillo. Minutes earlier, Carrillo, acting on a tipoff, had slipped away from the wedding.
Many of the mourners on Friday had also attended the wedding and were visibly nervous about the heavy military and police presence, saying they had been badly treated in January.
Officers and senior police commanders on the scene refused to answer reporters questions. No arrests were seen.

The death certificate issued for Carrillo gave the cause of death as a heart attack, but the local Televisa television network quoted an unnamed hospital source as saying Carrillo had been murdered by one of his bodyguards after the surgery.

The head of Mexico's anti-drug agency, Mariano Herran Salvatti said officials had ruled out suffocation as the cause of death but did not know if Carrillo might have been murdered by other means, such as a lethal injection.

He said four doctors, three not from Mexico City's private Santa Monica hospital, had performed the surgery and two heavily armed bodyguards had kept watch over the drug lord, keeping hospital staff away.
Mexican authorities were questioning the doctors, he said.
